4263.heavy: Not applicable (no stress). The source treats syllable weight, "usually typified by a contrast between long and short vowels" (p. 89), as a prosodic property of many Chadic languages that interacts with tone and intonation, not as a stress-attracting property; nothing weight-related is said of Miya stress.
4263.prule: Miya is a terraced-level tone language: tonal domains carry one of three lexical specifications, Toneless (T), High (H) or Low (L), realised by phrase-sensitive rules (T -> H phrase-initially, else copies the preceding pitch; H -> downstepped H after any material; L everywhere L; plus L-RAISING of a single L syllable after a L in its own domain unless it begins in a voiced obstruent); downsteps stack, and root-internal downsteps occur. No word-stress rule exists for Miya: the author (also the author of the only Miya grammar) states for the whole Chadic family that stress is not a prosodic parameter and that prosodic amplitude is a function of tone, syllable weight and intonation.
4263.srule: Not mentioned in Schuh 2017 (Ch. 1 §4 p. 6, Ch. 5 §1 p. 89 and §4.3 pp. 124-126 read): the source denies stress as a prosodic parameter for every Chadic language, so there is no secondary stress to state; the Miya section describes tone only.

tn.quote: Chaque syllabe porte un ton . Une étude morphotonologique s'avère bien entendu indispensable . Je n'ai pas trouvé d'oppositions permettant de poser l'existence de trois tons . Par contre, l'abaissement du ton haut est fréquent . Il semble systématique dans les verbes bi- ou trisyllabiques à la forme inaccomplie, lorsque les deux dernières syllabes sont de tons hauts . Le dernier est alors abaissé et s'oppose au ton bas de l'accompli lorsque la forme est par ailleurs similaire . nè wéésí [ nè wé: s1] “ je cherche " nè wéésì [ nè wé: sì] “ j'ai cherché " ...
tn.translation: Every syllable bears a tone. A morphotonological study is of course indispensable. I have found no oppositions that would allow positing three tones. On the other hand, lowering of the high tone is frequent. It seems systematic in bi- or trisyllabic verbs in the imperfective when the last two syllables are high-toned. The last one is then lowered and contrasts with the low tone of the perfective when the form is otherwise similar. nè wéésí 'I am looking for' / nè wéésì 'I looked for' ...
tn.cite: Rongier, Jacques. 1996. Aperçu sur le mɔyɔbɛ. Cahiers voltaïques / Gur Papers 1: 115-145
tn.locator: Phonologie section, tone paragraph (follows 'Syllabes'); page not returned by view (within pp. 115-145)
tn.note: Two level tones (high, low), one per syllable; no evidence for a third; final H lowered in imperfective verbs, contrasting with perfective L. Count of 2 implied, not stated. Pali 2011 posits H, M, L.

4264.cfw: Rongier 1996 and Pali 2011 both describe Miyobe as a tone language in which a high versus low tone on the verb marks aspect, and neither mentions word stress; they differ only on whether a third, mid tone level exists, and only excerpts of Rongier 1996 and the abstract of Pali 2011 are available.

4265.dloc: §2.2 超分節要素 and §2.3 音韻語, p. 43 (file page 3); §3.1 標識・接語・接辞, p. 48 (stressability of bound forms); §2.6 p. 48 (intonation = sentence level)
4265.prule: One stress per phonological word, on its final syllable (強勢位置は音韻語の最終音節である). Stress is non-contrastive and demarcative (marks phonological-word boundaries); quantity-insensitive: presyllables/minor syllables and non-final full syllables are unstressed whatever their shape, and vowel length is licensed by stress, not the reverse. Corroborated by Ito 2012: 48 (1.5+ syllable morphemes 'all iambic, stress always on the final syllable of the word') and Rischel 1982: 249 (multi-syllable lexemes: 'the last syllable seems to have always the main stress').
4265.srule: None: 「音韻語 1 つにつき、1 つの強勢を持つ。強勢位置は音韻語の最終音節である。」 ('each phonological word bears one stress, on its final syllable'); no secondary or rhythmic stress is described, and non-final (minor / unstressed) syllables are stressless (so also Ito 2012: 48). The earlier preliminary sketch Rischel 1982: 249 had left 'degrees of stress (e.g. weak versus secondary stress) on the non-final syllable(s)' undetermined.

4267.quote: Some important features like vowel length and tone will be examined in this chapter. Mmɛn like Aghem or many other Western grassfields languages is a tone language. It is a language in which both segmental and pitch phonemes, otherwise known as tones, go into the composition of words. It is known that in tone languages, words could either be distinguished on the basis of segments or/and tones; Mmɛn is no exception. The tones attested in the language are in some cases contrastive. [p. 67] ... III.2. Tones. There are principally five tones in Mmɛn namely - the high tone [ ´] - the mid tone [ ¯]…

4267.tone: Agha 1987 (the only dedicated phonology reachable) says nothing about stress or accent: the words 'stress', 'accent', 'prominence' do not occur in the 86 pp.; ch. III 'Suprasegmental phonology' (pp. 67-77) covers only III.1 Vowel length and III.2 Tones. Five tones: H, M, L, rising (LH), falling (HL), one per syllable; the two contour tones occur in 'barely one per cent of the total vocabulary' (p. 68); conclusion p. 77: 'Five suprasegmental phonemes (tones), three of which are level and two contour come up to confirm Mmɛn as a tone language.' Möller 2012 §3.2.1 gives underlying noun-root melodies H, L, HL, LH plus a surface M and uses 'accent marks' only as tone diacritics; Nilsson 2013:10 reports nine surface pitches on isolated syllables after Björkestedt 2011a:44. No source mentions stress.

tn.quote: Dermuha has four tones: high, mid, low and high-glottal. The high-glottal is relatively rare in the data compared to the other tones. The high tone is indicated by /˥/, the mid tone by /˧/, the low tone by /˩/ and the high glottal tone by /˥ˀ/. The high tone /˥/ starts at a high pitch but is slightly lower at the end. The high glottal /˥ˀ/ begins at a high pitch but falls slightly to low at the end and ends abruptly. The mid tone /˧/ is mid in pitch and vaguely drops at the end. The low tone /˩/ begins slightly lower than the mid tone and not dramatically falls to low at the end.

4270.qtr: I further note that, although in writing there is very much agreement between these languages, in speech very much difference exists. 4271.dq: L'accent et le schème tonal caractérisent également le mot phonologique mais sans lui conférer des limites aussi opératoires que le trait de palatalisation. Une syllabe finale est toujours accentuée devant pause (externe ou interne) (p. 445) ... Toute syllabe devant pause (interne ou externe) est accentuée ce qui entraîne la même règle d'épenthèse pausale (p. 456)
4271.dloc: Livre 1, chapter 'Le mot phonologique': §2.1 Les frontières externes, p. 445; verbal complex p. 451; §4 Conclusion p. 456. Tonal accent: §4.7 'Schèmes tonals structurels: schèmes accentuels' pp. 365-366 and §8.4 p. 426.
4271.heavy: Not applicable: the pausal accent is explicitly quantity-insensitive ('sur la syllabe finale, ouverte ou fermée'); the lexical prominence is tonal.
4271.prule: Two-tone language (registers H and B, only H marked). Each basic, non-derived word carries at most one H tone, which Barreteau reinterprets as a lexically placed 'accent tonal': absent (BB, BBB), initial (HB, HBB), internal (BHB) or final (BH, BBH), i.e. a pitch-accent-style analysis of lexical tone, not a stress rule. Separately, a non-distinctive 'accent d'intensité' falls automatically on the final syllable (open or closed) of the phonological word before a pause, external or internal.
4271.srule: Only in reduplicated words: the simple (non-derived) phonological word has a single, non-distinctive intensity accent on its final syllable before pause; in adjectivo-adverbals and nouns derived by full or partial reduplication, the final syllable of each reduplicated part before the internal (virtual or semi-) pause is also accented (daf-daf-dafaf 'épais'), the internal accent disappearing in rapid speech; prefix mV- and initial CV- reduplication take no pause. No primary/secondary ranking and no rhythmic stress is described.
4271.quote: Une syllabe finale est toujours accentuée devant pause (externe ou interne): elle est prononcée avec plus de force et surtout, elle est toujours vocalisée, qu'elle se termine par une syllabe ouverte: (C)CV, ou fermée: (C)CVC. C'est ainsi que nous analysons les syllabes finales (C)CVC comme des réalisations pausales accentuées de (C)CC avec épenthèse. La position de l'accent d'intensité est fixe et systématique devant pause; il n'est donc pas distinctif. (p. 445) ... Devant pause, un accent d'intensité se porte automatiquement sur la syllabe finale, ouverte ou fermée, ce qui entraîne la règle …
4271.loc: Livre 1, chapter 'Le mot phonologique': §2.1 Les frontières externes, p. 445; verbal complex p. 451; §4 Conclusion p. 456. Tonal accent: §4.7 'Schèmes tonals structurels: schèmes accentuels' pp. 365-366 and §8.4 p. 426.

Nous avons effectué un autre séjour au Cameroun, de 1979 à 1981.'…
4271.exq_: La position de l'accent d'intensité est fixe et systématique devant pause; il n'est donc pas distinctif. (p. 445)
4271.tone: Two tone registers H and B, only H marked (p. 353). Basic words carry at most one H, reinterpreted as an 'accent tonal' (pp. 365-366, 426); H entails vowel tension. The 1983 thesis §4.2-4.3 (pp. 374-376) formalises [+haut] -> [+accent] and states 'il conviendrait de distinguer deux types d'accent: l'accent tonal et l'accent d'intensité, l'accent tonal impliquant celui d'intensité mais non pas l'inverse'; §4.1 (p. 373): 'Les syllabes finales de mot (ouvertes ou fermées) sont toujours accentuées devant pause... quel que soit le ton de celle-ci.' Hollingsworth 1980 p. 1: Mofu-Gudur 'is a tonal language which also exhibits stress'; p. 9: 'while a tonal language, also has stress which influences the tone on the word, phrase, and sentence levels. On an utterance in a discourse stress is frequently predictable on the basis of grammatical criteria' -- his 'stress' is speaker-assigned information focus (super-high pitch), not a word-level position.

tn.quote: 1.1. Le trait de hauteur ... concerne uniquement les segments syllabiques, c'est-à-dire les voyelles, et toutes les voyelles sont caractérisées par un ton. ... 1.2. Nous observons deux registres tonals, qui se confondent avec les tonèmes, haut (H) et bas (B). ... tn.translation: 1.1. The pitch feature concerns only the syllabic segments, i.e. the vowels, and all vowels are characterised by a tone. ... 1.2. We observe two tonal registers, which coincide with the tonemes, high (H) and low (B). ... Since the language uses only two phonological tones, in transcriptions we shall mark only the high tone (the less frequent) and leave the low tone unmarked.

4274.dq: Pada akhir kata, kadang-kadang terdapat vokal yang panjang, dan vokal itulah yang ditekankan. ... Bahasa Moma memiliki beberapa enklitik ... yang diucapkan sama seperti akhiran tetapi tidak mempengaruhi ucapan kata dasarnya. ... Suku kata yang tebal ditekankan.
4274.dloc: 'Petunjuk' (Ejaan Percobaan Bahasa Moma-Kulawi): p. x, paragraph 'VOKAL PANJANG'; p. xi, paragraph 'LAIPEKUNEMU'I' (enclitics); 'Pololita Eo-eona / Percakapan Sehari-hari', note p. 249 (pp. 14, 15, 269).
4274.heavy: A long vowel at the end of the word ('Pada akhir kata, kadang-kadang terdapat vokal yang panjang, dan vokal itulah yang ditekankan'), written with two vowel letters: hamaa, paletaa, toronaa, humpii, woo, mpuu. The source adds only that long vowels do not occur at the beginning of a word ('Vokal panjang tidak terdapat pada awal kata panjang'); it does not say they are absent non-finally, and its own stress marking shows base-final long vowels before enclitics inside the written word, all carrying the stress (para[luu]ku, para[luu]ta, para[luu]mu, para[luu]kudi, [wuu]ku, po’o[haa]ta, Natoro[naa]’adapa), so 'end of the word' means the end of the word minus enclitics. The bold marking also treats final diphthongs as one stressed unit ([hou], [rau], tu[mai], We[lau], Na[bai], [hei], [ei]).
4274.dflt: Penultimate syllable of the word including suffixes, excluding enclitics. Not stated in prose in the open source; established by the source's own stress marking (independent tally over 286 bold-marked Moma tokens in pp. 249-263: 170 penult of the written word, 60 penult of the base once an enclitic string is set aside, 27 'final' = final long vowel/diphthong units, monosyllables and I[yo], 29 residue that are mostly enclitic-stripping misses of the crude script, e.g. Me[ha]nitamo, tu[a]kaku, ro[du]amo; the compilers tally with hand-checked enclitics gives 298/304 penult) and stated in words second-hand by Himmelmann & Kaufman 2020 (Google Books): 'prominence is associated with the penultimate syllable of the word including suffixes but excluding pronominal and adverbial clitics. Enclitics do not attract prominence even when they are disyllabic, as in ['hou=kami]' citing Adriani & Esser 1939: 9.
4274.prule: Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word, counting suffixes but not enclitics; a long vowel (written VV) at the end of the word minus enclitics, or a final diphthong, is itself stressed. Equivalently: stress on the penultimate mora of the word minus enclitics.

4275.dq: On non-monosyllabic words only two levels are contrastive, and these on the stressed syllable only.
4275.dloc: Endnote 1, pp. 201-202; also p. 187 examples (6)-(7) for tone marks on polysyllables
4275.prule: No stress-placement rule stated. Momuna is described as a tone language: three contrastive tone levels (high, mid, low) on monosyllables; on polysyllabic words a two-way tone contrast carried by the stressed syllable only. The note presupposes one stressed syllable per polysyllabic word but never says where it falls or whether its position is predictable.
4275.quote: Momuna phonemes are orthographically symbolised as follows: the stops t, k, b; the liquid r; the sibilant s; the nasals m, n; the semi-vowels w, y; the labialised stops bw, kw; the palatalised consonants sy, by, ny; the vowels i, ee (close mid front), e (open mid front), a, o (low back), oo (close mid back), u; the diphthongs ei, ai, oi, au, ou. There are three levels of contrastive tone on monosyllables: high (marked by the acute accent), mid (unmarked) and low (marked by a grave accent). On non-monosyllabic words only two levels are contrastive, and these on the stressed syllable only.
4275.loc: Endnote 1, pp. 201-202; also p. 187 examples (6)-(7) for tone marks on polysyllables
4275.idn: Momuna (originally called 'Somahai'), Papuan language spoken between the Balim and Kolff River systems, Kabupaten Jayawijaya, Irian Jaya (Indonesia); data: Note 1, p. 202: 'The present study was undertaken in a workshop held in 1984 in Danau Bira, Irian Jaya with the Cooperative Program of Cenderawasih University and…
4275.tone: Three contrastive tone levels on monosyllables (high = acute, mid = unmarked, low = grave); on polysyllables only two levels contrast, and only on the stressed syllable, i.e. tone contrast is culminative on the stressed syllable (compatible with a pitch-accent-type analysis, but Reimer calls it tone and gives no stress rule). The text examples mark tone on polysyllables: p. 187 ex. (6) 'Máenee', 'Rúenee' (acute on the first vowel of both names) and ex. (7) 'kì' (grave on a monosyllable); two proper names are too few to read a placement pattern off. Usher (New Guinea World, second-hand from Reimer 1986 and an unpublished Reimer n.d. phonology) restates it as two tones 'on the vowel which carries primary stress' and notes that Reimer's materials mark high and low tones on disyllables without explanation.

4278.heavy: A syllable containing a two-vowel cluster /VV/ (/ii yy uu ee aa oo yi ui ei ai oi/), each /V/ counted separately in the right-to-left count (condition 107c(1) 'a single /V/ (not /VV/)' confirms /VV/ syllables are the heavy class); and the word-final syllable when the word ends in /C/. 4278.dflt: V-final all-light words: penult, then every second syllable leftward (4 syllables 1010; 5 syllables 01010 with weak stress on the initial syllable; a 10010 unit only under the 107c conditions); C-final all-light words: final syllable. Stress is never on the antepenult with both following syllables unstressed.
4278.prule: Right-edge mora count. In a V-final word the stressed syllable is the one containing the next-to-last /V/: the penult when the last two syllables are CV, but a final syllable with a /VV/ cluster (long vowel or diphthong, counted as two /V/) takes the stress itself; in a C-final word the final syllable is stressed. Word-level primary = this rightmost computed stress; it becomes 'strong' stress only when it is the last stressed syllable before the intonational juncture /./ (i.e. in isolation or phrase-finally), otherwise it is 'intermediate'.
4278.srule: Iterative right-to-left by vowel count from the primary stress: the syllable containing the second /V/ before a stressed syllable is stressed, and so on leftward (each /V/ of a /VV/ cluster counts, so CV syllables alternate and a CVV syllable next to a stress is itself stressed); these are 'intermediate' stresses (§107d); an initial syllable not reached by the count has 'weak' stress (§107b); under four segmental conditions (§107c) a stress stands on the third syllable before a stressed one, never at the word end.

4283.prule: Primary (lexical) stress falls regularly on the penultimate syllable of every polysyllabic word; placement is insensitive to syllable quantity (vowel length or coda do not attract stress).
4283.srule: In long polysynthetic words (the source: structures 'above five or six syllables') secondary stresses fall on every second syllable leftward from the penultimate primary stress, i.e. quantity-insensitive right-to-left trochaic feet: [nik.ˌkʷah.kʷal.ˌt͡ɬaʃ.kal.ˈma.ka] 'I give him/her beautiful tortillas' (7 syllables: secondary on 2 and 4, primary on 6, initial syllable unfooted). The author's dedicated study (Velázquez Patiño 2014, in Herrera Zendejas ed., p. 110-112, 119, 136) marks the same placement in 5-syllable (syllable 2) and 7-syllable (syllables 2, 4) verb complexes.

4285.tone: Persson 2004 p. 84: Bongo, Jur Mödö and Morokodo 'all have two-tone systems similar to Baka'; for Baka 'there are two contrasting tones and all high tones are indicated by an acute accent over the vowel'; the Morokodo committee chose not to mark tone in the 1999 orthography because 'context was adequate to decide the meaning in all but a few cases'. Nothing on stress or accent placement for Morokodo anywhere in the article (a full-text search of the article text for stress/accent/prosod returns only the acute-accent tone-marking sentence and the Jur Mödö syllable paragraph on p. 80). The only 'stress' passages in the OPSL 9 issue are in other articles (Dinka and Nuer orthography papers), not about Morokodo. The tone characterisation is a one-sentence, orthography-survey remark, not a word-level tonal analysis; the sister-language Jur Mödö sketch (p. 80) gives two level tones per syllable with glides on long vowels, but the author does not extend that detail to Morokodo. PHOIBLE inventory 1424 (Green & Moran, from Persson 2004) lists two tones H and L, no stress (second-hand).

4287.prule: Tone language: four phonemic tones (High, Low, High-falling, Low-falling) plus a polar-question high-rising tone and downstep; tone marks case, number and TAM. Stress or pitch accent is said to exist phonetically but to be non-distinctive; no placement rule is given anywhere in the sketch.

4287.tone: Source describes Akie as tonal (H, L, HF, LF; high-rising only in polar questions; downstep) with tone carrying case (accusative vs nominative), noun number and verbal TAM contrasts, and gives two tone-sandhi rules (HF > H / _L; L > H / #_L in fluent speech). The single remark on stress: 'Stress, or pitch accent, clearly exists but does not appear to phonologically distinctive' (p. 25, verbatim incl. the missing 'be'). Narrow phonetic transcriptions carry a stress mark in varying positions (e.g. [ˈʔàmdɪ̀] 'food', [kàˈlíːsyà] 'Kalisya', [ˈkárɪkà] 'woman', [wàˈárɛ̀ː] 'children', [ʔàˈŋkûn] 'I know') without any comment, so no positional rule can be inferred from the source.

tn.quote: 2.3 Tones The following tones are distinguished as phonemic units: Label Abbreviation Marking Example High H accute accent (e.g., á) káé ‘Look there!’ Low L unmarked (e.g., a) kaaʊ ‘homestead’ High-falling HF circumflex (e.g., â) yâ ‘bad’ Low-falling LF (e.g., ȁ) kɛ̏ɛn̏ ‘oneself’ In addition there is a high-rising tone (ʺ), restricted to polar questions (see Section 3.7.3.1). ... Tone is a feature mainly associated with vowels, and long vowels are interpreted as carrying two tone units. ... Finally, there is a tonal downstep (marked with a preceding exclamation mark)

corr.words: Nevertheless, it may be distinctive, e.g., in case marking. Thus, case of the quantifier ‘all’ below is distinguished only by whether there is a final low (a) or low-falling tone (b): (a) tukul ‘all (accusative)’ (b) tukȕl ‘all (nominative)’ ... (a) HF > H│_ L A high-falling tone (HF) changes to high tone (H) when followed by a low tone (L) ... (b) L > H│#_ L A low tone (L) changes to high (H) in fluent speech if followed by a low tone in the next word
